claims.text: The infant remains at risk for early-onset sepsis given persistent fever, tachypnea, and poor feeding despite a negative culture at 36 hours.
Continue hourly vital sign monitoring, including temperature, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation, and reassess feeding tolerance every 4 hours.
Repeat a full blood count and CRP at 48 hours to assess for evolving inflammatory markers, as CRP has moderate sensitivity for neonatal sepsis.
Escalate to intensive care if the infant develops worsening tachypnea, chest indrawing, or hypoxia (SpO₂ < 94 %) within the next 12 hours.

Maintain empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics until 48 hours of culture negativity and clinical stability, then consider de-escalation if repeat cultures remain negative and inflammatory markers decline.
Plan a follow-up assessment at 72 hours to evaluate clinical improvement and laboratory trends before deciding on antibiotic discontinuation.

claims.text: The WHO 2024 serious bacterial infections guidance does not provide evidence that a 36‑hour culture‑negative infant remains at high risk of early‑onset sepsis; it reports no evidence for culture‑confirmed sepsis as a reference standard.
The WHO guidance does not specify a NICE‑style 36‑hour stopping pathway for empiric antibiotics in infants with negative cultures.

The WHO guidance reports that the 7‑sign IMCI algorithm has fair sensitivity and specificity for detecting sepsis in infants 0–59 days, but it does not recommend a specific repeat laboratory testing schedule.
The WHO guidance does not provide specific vital sign monitoring frequency or escalation thresholds for infants with suspected sepsis.
The WHO guidance does not define ICU escalation criteria such as worsening tachypnea, chest indrawing, or hypoxia within a set timeframe.
The WHO guidance does not recommend a 72‑hour follow‑up assessment to decide on antibiotic discontinuation.
The WHO guidance indicates that CRP has moderate sensitivity (≈0.62) and specificity (≈0.74) for diagnosing neonatal sepsis, but it does not prescribe a 48‑hour repeat testing interval.
The WHO guidance notes that diagnostic accuracy studies for laboratory biomarkers in infants 0–59 days are limited and that no single biomarker reliably rules out sepsis.

The WHO guidance highlights that clinical sign‑based algorithms for PSBI in young infants have fair sensitivity and specificity, but their performance is compared against physician judgement rather than culture confirmation.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY

patient.clinical_condition: hospitalized with suspected sepsis and persistent signs

packet.evaluation_question: Hospitalized suspected sepsis: a culture is negative at 36 hours but clinical signs persist. Does this WHO source provide a NICE-style 36-hour stopping pathway? Gestation 35 weeks; age 63 hours; setting hospital.

evidence.text: 0–6 days: Good sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture- confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.

0–59 days and 7–59 days: Fair sensitivity and fair specificity ᵃ of the 7-sign IMCI algorithm compared with physician judgement of sepsis as the reference standard; there was no evidence for either culture-confirmed sepsis or mortality as the reference standard.

Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

Question: Among young infants aged 0–59 days with PSBI, in non-hospital settings, what is the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of clinical sign-based algorithms of PSBIᵃ compared with a reference standard (culture-confirmed sepsis, physician judgement of sepsis, or mortality) in identifying infants who require treatment for PSBI?
